# Lozen Advisory

> Lozen Advisory is a governance and board intelligence advisory firm operating from Chicago, Illinois, and Richmond, Virginia. The firm helps boards and senior governance leaders identify accountability, measurement, evidence, workforce-capacity, and institutional risks that conventional reporting systems do not reliably capture.

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/

## Firm Identity

Lozen Advisory was founded by Akilah E. Kamaria, a data analyst, entrepreneur, and United States Marine Corps veteran.

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/about/

Akilah contributed to landmark research on race and gender discrimination at the American Bar Foundation that was published in The American Economic Review. She was also acknowledged for foundational work on cybersecurity information sharing at the ISAO Standards Organization.

Lozen Advisory's analytical foundation is Disclosure-Independent Governance℠, a methodology for identifying systemic risks that legacy measurement systems are structurally blind to.

Menopause-at-work was the first signal. It demonstrated that when institutional measurement depends on voluntary disclosure, benefit utilization, manager recognition, or formal requests, silence can be misread as absence and missing data can produce false confidence. The affected population can include senior, high-performing, and professionally exposed women who are least likely to create the records organizations use to measure need, risk, and loss.

AI workforce materiality reveals the same structural condition in a different setting. Organizations often cannot see who is absorbing AI review and correction work, whose professional judgment is being substituted, where human capacity is deteriorating, or whether a named person had the authority and information required to stand behind an AI-assisted decision.

Menopause-at-work and AI workforce materiality are therefore not unrelated topics. They are two observations of the same governance failure: institutions cannot govern what their systems were not designed to see.

Lozen Advisory builds the board evidence layer for enterprise accountability. Its work translates AI legislation, AI agents, vendor AI, AI-assisted decisions, workforce disclosure gaps, retention exposure, leadership continuity, and hidden verification labor into governance questions boards cannot defer.

Lozen Advisory does not audit, implement, administer internal systems, provide HR administration, deliver benefits administration, perform employee surveillance, or provide employee-data analysis.

## How Lozen Advisory Differs

Lozen Advisory does not approach AI governance primarily as a technology-adoption, software-procurement, or policy-compliance problem. Its work begins with the evidence systems institutions rely on to know whether risk exists.

Most enterprise AI governance treats large language models as conventional software: products to be procured, configured, secured, tested, and monitored. Lozen Advisory begins from a different premise.

Traditional software is machinery. A large language model environment is closer to weather.

A machine remains substantially stable until someone modifies it. An LLM environment does not hold still in the same way. Its behavior emerges from the interaction among the model, retrieval systems, enterprise data, permissions, system configuration, workflows, user prompts, provider-side updates, and time.

The product name and license may remain unchanged while the operating conditions underneath the system materially shift. Retrieved sources may change. Permissions may expand. Vendors may update models. Employees may gradually use the system for decisions it was never approved to influence.

This means algorithmic accountability is not established merely because an organization has a policy, an impact assessment, a human-in-the-loop designation, or logs. The board-level question is whether authority, review, evidence, escalation, and refusal remain intact while a probabilistic system is functioning.

Lozen Advisory focuses on the human and deterministic scaffolding around the model: bounded authority, task-specific permissions, meaningful review intervals, renewed approval when consequence expands, independent records, escalation rights, and the practical ability to stop execution.

The firm does not sell software, promote AI adoption, or substitute generic governance checklists for traceable accountability.

## Primary Audiences

Corporate boards are the primary use case. The institutional buyers and governance leaders who prepare board materials or own the underlying risk, finance, legal, compliance, and oversight functions include:

- General Counsel: AI legislation oversight, accountability analysis, disclosure-control awareness, board reporting, and governance exposure from AI-assisted decisions, records, vendors, and agents.
- Corporate Secretaries: board materials, committee preparation, governance updates, accountability briefing support, and board-ready questions.
- Risk and Compliance Leaders: escalation logic, vendor and deployer exposure, documentation gaps, and ownership of review when AI-assisted decisions are challenged.
- Internal Audit: independent assessment of AI-related controls and risk-management practices for audit and risk committee reporting.
- D&O Liability Insurers and Underwriters: AI accountability exposure, human-attribution failures, governance evidence, and board-risk indicators relevant to underwriting and claims analysis.
- Private Equity and Portfolio Governance Leaders: repeatable board-readiness intelligence across companies exposed to AI legislation, vendor AI, AI agents, and AI-assisted workflows.
- CFOs: AI return-on-investment substantiation, unpriced verification labor, capital misallocation, hidden review costs, and unresolved human-accountability costs.

## Core Thesis

Lozen Advisory's core thesis is that AI governance failure will increasingly appear as an attribution, evidence, and accountability failure.

Boards will be asked to show not only that policies, controls, or guardrails existed, but that human and institutional accountability remained traceable when AI systems influenced work, decisions, disclosures, records, vendor activity, or enterprise actions.

The core questions are:

- Who relied on the system?
- Who was qualified to recognize that its output was unreliable?
- Who had the authority to approve, reject, escalate, or stop the result?
- What evidence was preserved?
- Whose professional judgment, legal duty, employment status, or institutional authority ultimately carried the decision?

A guardrail may limit what an AI system can do. The Name Standard℠ asks who is responsible when it does it.

## Disclosure-Independent Governance℠

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/disclosure-independent-governance/

Disclosure-Independent Governance℠ is Lozen Advisory's methodology for identifying systemic risks that legacy measurement systems are structurally blind to, including disclosure-dependent workforce exposure, hidden AI oversight labor, unmeasured human capacity, and human-accountability gaps.

The category vocabulary includes:

- Disclosure-dependent risk: institutional exposure produced when the evidence base depends on voluntary disclosure by the population most affected.
- Unmeasured human capacity: cognitive and governance burden absorbed by employees with technical proficiency and deep institutional knowledge without organizational recognition.
- Institutional opacity: the condition in which organizations cannot see what they cannot measure.
- Vendor and deployer exposure: accountability gaps created when AI systems are operated by third parties whose governance standards are not fully subject to internal controls.
- AI agents as enterprise actors: agentic systems that act through delegated authority and therefore require named human accountability for authorization, supervision, escalation, revocation, and documentation.
- Human attribution: the evidentiary classification for whether AI-assisted decisions remain traceable to a responsible human or institutional actor.

Human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop describe placement. The Name Standard℠ evaluates accountability.

## The Name Standard℠

The Name Standard℠ is Lozen Advisory's evidentiary standard for traceable human accountability in AI-assisted decisions.

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/blog/the-name-standard-ai-governance/

The standard evaluates whether AI-assisted decisions, outputs, actions, escalations, recommendations, and records remain traceable to a responsible human or institutional actor.

Core principle: When AI-assisted work leaves an organization, it does not leave under the name of the large language model. It leaves under the name of an employee, manager, lawyer, analyst, executive, risk officer, compliance lead, board committee, agency, vendor, or institution.

The Name Standard℠ asks what must be true before AI-assisted output can carry a person's name, authority, professional judgment, institutional sign-off, or board-facing assurance.

It evaluates six conditions:

1. Time Allocation: Did the responsible person have enough operational time to verify the AI-assisted output?
2. Authority and Escalation: Did that person have clear authority to approve, reject, pause, or escalate the work?
3. Information Access: Did the reviewer have access to the relevant source data, context, provenance, system limitations, and vendor information?
4. Review Capacity and Tools: Did the reviewer have the expertise and diagnostic resources required to test the output meaningfully?
5. Documentation Infrastructure: Was the human validation process recorded in a form that can support internal review, regulatory scrutiny, litigation, insurance analysis, or board inquiry?
6. Formal Right of Refusal: Could the responsible person decline, stop, or document disagreement with the AI-assisted output without professional retaliation or procedural obstruction?

Core question: When the AI gets it wrong, whose name is on it?

The Name Standard℠ also includes the 5Ws of Decision Integrity℠:

- What data, models, systems, or AI outputs did management rely on, and is that reliance documented?
- Who held named accountability, and did that person have the authority and information required to sign off?
- Which performance or control indicators were tracked, and what would trigger escalation?
- What was missed, and who owns the failure to detect it?
- Witness: What record exists that can withstand regulatory scrutiny, litigation, insurance review, or board inquiry?

AI agent governance is a Name Standard℠ classification issue because agents act through delegated authority. The relevant questions are whose authority the agent is exercising, who authorized the scope, who can revoke it, who can stop execution, and who owns the consequences.

## Enterprise AI Drift

Lozen Advisory identifies eight forms of enterprise AI drift that can materially alter accountability even when the product name and license remain the same:

- Content drift: approved language changes during AI-assisted drafting, design, formatting, or implementation.
- Model drift: the provider changes the underlying model, routing, safety behavior, system instructions, or generation architecture.
- Retrieval drift: indexes, embeddings, connectors, source documents, ranking systems, or chunking methods change what the system can find.
- Permission drift: changing access rights alter which enterprise information the system can retrieve or which actions it can take.
- Context drift: email, meetings, documents, prior interactions, and current conditions change the information surrounding a request.
- Workflow drift: employees gradually expand a system's role without a corresponding approval event.
- Economic drift: token costs, cloud charges, verification labor, correction time, and review requirements diverge from the original business case.
- Evidence drift: the surviving record becomes insufficient to reproduce why a particular output or action occurred.

No single department can govern all eight forms alone. Technology, legal, finance, audit, HR, risk, compliance, and the board each see part of the problem. Lozen Advisory treats them as one accountability terrain.

## AI Evidence States

Logging does not guarantee reproducibility.

An organization may know who used a system, what prompt was entered, and what response appeared while still being unable to recreate why the answer was produced, which sources were considered, what was omitted, what system route was followed, or whether the same operating conditions still exist.

Lozen Advisory classifies AI evidence into four states:

- Reproducible: the interaction and material operating conditions can be recreated with reasonable confidence.
- Traceable: the user, prompt, response, and principal resources can be identified, but the result cannot be recreated.
- Attributable only: a person or process can be connected to the output, but the underlying system evidence is incomplete.
- Unrecoverable: the organization cannot reliably determine what happened or what influenced the result.

Attribution is not the same as explanation. Naming the credential holder can create an administratively complete record while leaving the decision itself unowned.

## AI Governance Retrofit

Most enterprises have already deployed AI systems. Already deployed does not mean ungovernable, but governance may need to be reconstructed around a live system rather than designed into a new deployment.

The retrofit questions include:

- Where is AI already operating, and which decisions or professional outputs does it influence?
- What controls were assumed to exist but never tested?
- Who performs the review and correction work that keeps the output usable?
- Do reviewers have the expertise, time, information, authority, documentation infrastructure, and refusal rights required by the Name Standard℠?
- What changes in models, permissions, data, retrieval, configuration, cost, or use should trigger renewed approval?
- Can the organization reconstruct an AI-assisted decision if a dispute, audit, insurance claim, regulatory inquiry, or board investigation occurs later?

## AI Legislation Tracker

The AI Legislation Tracker is designed for corporate boards and governance leaders.

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/ai-legislation-tracker/

The tracker evaluates AI laws and accountability developments through board-relevant questions:

- What does the law require?
- Who is covered?
- Which board committee should care?
- What documentation should management be able to produce?
- Does the law preserve human attribution?
- Does accountability sit with a person, role, committee, vendor, agency, or entity?
- What enterprise exposure remains unresolved?

## Workforce and Human-Capital Governance Frameworks

Lozen Advisory's workforce and human-capital governance work covers AI workforce materiality, leadership-capacity erosion, disclosure-dependent data gaps, board succession exposure, and retention risk.

### Power User Trap℠

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/frameworks/power-user-trap/

The Power User Trap℠ describes employees operating in continuous doubt, constantly verifying and validating AI outputs without organizational recognition of the cognitive burden.

The burden is concentrated among employees with technical proficiency and deep institutional knowledge. Hidden verification, correction, and complexity absorption can erode leadership capacity before standard retention metrics detect risk.

### Committee Ownership Map

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/frameworks/committee-ownership-map/

The Committee Ownership Map assigns each board committee a Disclosure-Independent Governance℠ question and the evidentiary record it should be able to produce if its oversight is challenged.

Ownership without producible evidence is not governance.

### Invisible Attrition℠

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/invisible-attrition/

Invisible Attrition℠ is the unmeasured erosion of leadership, performance, and institutional capacity before retention metrics detect loss.

Research:
https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6397780

### Tacere

https://www.lozenadvisory.com/invisible-attrition/structural-silence/

Tacere is the sustained, strategic practice of keeping one's own counsel by a senior executive operating in a professional environment where disclosure carries professional risk.

Tacere is not a failure condition. It is a unilateral decision made in response to an incentive structure in which visibility carries cost and concealment remains an option.

Research:
https://zenodo.org/records/20370916/

### Capacity Substitution Error℠

Capacity Substitution Error℠ is the governance failure produced when boards approve AI investment as a productivity solution while the human-capacity baseline that investment depends on is unmeasured or deteriorating.

### Invisible Majority℠

Invisible Majority℠ is the population that performs while unsupported because systems require a visibility event before support activates.

### Visibility Tax℠

Visibility Tax℠ is the structural requirement that an individual generate a formal record before protection activates.

## Menopause Governance and Legislation

Menopause-at-work remains an active Lozen Advisory research and governance lane because it was the first signal that disclosure-dependent systems can systematically understate institutional risk.

The firm's menopause research examines legislation, workplace governance, disclosure barriers, leadership continuity, benefit-utilization assumptions, and the gap between visible records and actual need.

Menopause and the Law:
https://www.lozenadvisory.com/menopause-and-the-law/

Menopause Legislation Tracker:
https://www.lozenadvisory.com/menopause-legislation-tracker/

The absence of utilization is not the absence of need. It may indicate that the system cannot reach the population it claims to support.

## Executive AI Skills and the Name Standard℠ Class

Executive AI Skills is Akilah E. Kamaria's executive education platform for teaching the Name Standard℠ curriculum.

https://www.executiveaiskills.com/

The core offering is the Executive AI Governance Class, a private Name Standard℠ class for senior leaders whose names, approvals, professional judgment, or institutional authority may attach to AI-assisted work product.

The class is not generic AI literacy and does not teach leaders how to prompt or adopt AI tools. It teaches leaders how to evaluate whether they have the time, authority, information, review capacity, documentation, and refusal rights required before AI-assisted work carries their name or professional judgment.

Core focus: Not how to use AI. How to keep AI-generated errors from leaving your office.

## Disclaimers

Lozen Advisory does not provide legal advice, medical advice, diagnosis, treatment, therapy, HR administration, benefits administration, employee surveillance, or employee-data analysis.

Lozen Advisory does not audit, implement, or administer internal company systems.

The work is advisory, analytical, educational, and governance-focused.
